Others said: it is a reference to the expiation of the oath connected with the prohibition. "Al-tahillah" is a verbal noun, its form being "taf'ilah," and it was assimilated (idghām) due to the coming together of two identical letters. In this verse, He referred to the explanation of feeding in the expiation of an oath by God, the Exalted, in another verse. "Al-mawla" is the one who gives support, the helper and aider.

The majority said: "al-hadith" is his saying ﷺ concerning the matter of Mariyah. Others said: it is only his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I only drank honey." Her informing was to 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, and this, and what is similar to it, is the collusion (tazahur) for which they were both rebuked. When they enter upon a full sentence, they are transitive to three objects, and it is not permissible to limit them. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and God made it known to him﴾ means: He informed him.

So God's knowledge is a guarantee of their requital, and likewise the Prophet's knowledge. The meaning with the doubled ra' is: he informed him of it and made it binding upon him. His saying, the Exalted: "and he turned away from some" means: out of generosity, modesty and good companionship. al-Hasan said: "No noble person has ever insisted on full detail." It has been narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ at that time divorced Hafsah, may God be pleased with her, then God, the Exalted, (p. 342) commanded him to take her back. It has also been narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ rebuked her and did not divorce her. When she informed the Messenger of God ﷺ of the news and that she had disclosed it to 'A'ishah, she thought that 'A'ishah had exposed her, so she said: "Who told you this?" in the manner of seeking verification. When he informed her that God, the Exalted, had told him, she fell silent and submitted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 66, verse 4–5:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts have indeed inclined; but if you back each other up against him, then indeed Allah is his Protector, and Jibril and the righteous among the believers, and the angels after that are supporters.﴾ ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you: submitting (muslimat), believing (mu'minat), devoutly obedient (qanitat), repentant (ta'ibat), worshipping ('abidat), traveling (sa'ihat), previously married (thayyibat) and virgins (abkaran).﴾

The address in His saying, ﴿If you two turn in repentance to Allah﴾, is to Hafsa and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both. In the hadith of al-Bukhari and others, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: I said to 'Umar: "Who are the two women who backed each other up against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He said: "Hafsa and 'A'isha." His saying, ﴿your hearts have indeed inclined﴾, means: they deviated from uprightness and rightness. Al-saghw (inclining) is inclination, and from it comes "saghiyat al-rajul" (a man's entourage), namely his companions who incline toward him; and from it: "asgha ilayhi bi-sam'ihi" (he inclined his ear to him), and "asgha al-inaa'" (he tilted the vessel). In the recitation of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "fa-qad zaghat qulubukuma" (your hearts have swerved), and al-zaygh is inclination, though its common usage is in opposition to the truth. Mujahid said: "We used to consider 'sagh' (inclined) to be a minor matter until we heard the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: 'zaghat' (swerved)." The plural "qulub" (hearts) for two is a plural in terms of what is possible, and there is no ambiguity in the wording; this is like the saying of the poet:

﴾ ............... their backs are like the backs of two shields

The meaning of the verse: if you repent, then there has already occurred from you what ought to be repented of. This response, which is the answer to the condition, is in meaning prior, though it is placed as the answer in wording. "In tazahara" means: if you cooperate. The "ta'" was assimilated into the "za'" after it was changed (into a "za'"). 'Ikrima, the mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, read it with two "ta's" in accordance with the original form. The Kufans, Talha, Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read it with the "za'" lightened by dropping one of the "ta's." It is related from Ibn 'Umar that he read it with the "za'" and "ha'" doubled without an alif. "Al-mawla" means the helper and supporter.

His saying, ﴿and Jibril and the righteous among the believers﴾, may be a conjunction with the name of Allah the Exalted in His saying "huwa" (He), so that ﴿and Jibril and the righteous among the believers﴾ is in the guardianship (walaya). It may also be that "Jibril" is in the nominative as the subject, and what follows it is coordinated with it, and "zahir" (supporters) is the predicate; in that case they are from the sense of support, not of guardianship, and it is specific that He, glory be to Him, is the Mawla of Allah.

People differed regarding "salih al-mu'minin" (the righteous among the believers). Al-Tabari and other scholars said: it is general, and every righteous person is included in it. Al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrima said: what is meant is Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, and Ibn Mas'ud related it from the Prophet ﷺ. Mujahid said something similar and also said: and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Salih al-mu'minin is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Qatada, al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad and others said: they are the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and this is only consistent if their support consists in their being exemplars and models, so they are helpers in this sense. His saying, ﴿and the righteous among the believers﴾, may be a singular collective noun, and it may be intended as "wa-salihu" (and the righteous ones), so the waw was dropped in the script of the Mushaf, as they dropped it in His saying: ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 18] and in other places.

It is related from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not be concerned about the matter of your wives, for Allah is with you, and Jibril is with you, and Abu Bakr is with you, and I am with you,' so the verse was revealed in agreement, roughly, with the saying of 'Umar." Al-Mahdawi said: It is related that this verse was revealed upon the tongue of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise it is related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: "It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you," and the verse was revealed in accordance with his words. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Umm Salama said to me: "O son of al-Khattab, you have inserted yourself into everything, until you have entered between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his wives," and she seized me with a grip by which she broke me. Zaynab bint Jahsh said to me: "O 'Umar, is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ not able to admonish his wives until you admonish them?"

The majority read ﴿ṭallaqakunna﴾ with a fatha on the qaf and clear pronunciation. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Ibn 'Abbas from him, read it with the qaf assimilated into the kaf and doubled. Abu 'Ali said: the assimilation of the qaf into the kaf is good. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, the Kufans, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿an yubdilahu﴾ with a sukun on the ba' and a lightened dal. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read ﴿an yubaddilahu﴾ with a fatha on the ba' and a doubled dal. This is the dialect of the Qur'an in this verb.

Allah the Exalted repeated the attributes for emphasis, although some of them include others: "islam" refers to affirmation and action, while "iman" is a specification and an alert to its noble standing. "Qanitat" means obedient. "Al-sa'ihat" was said to mean fasting; this was said by Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak, and al-Zajjaj mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ said it. It was also said to mean emigrants (muhajirat); this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Zayd said: there is no wandering (siyaha) in Islam except emigration. It was also said to mean those who go forth in the obedience of Allah. The fasting person is likened to the wanderer in that the wanderer is absorbed and does not look for provisions or food; likewise the fasting person refrains from that, so he and the wanderer are equal in abstention and in hardship of life due to the lack of food. His saying, ﴿thayyibat wa-abkaran﴾ (previously married and virgins), is a division of each of the preceding attributes. This waw is not one of those of which it may be said "the waw of eight," because here it is necessary; if it were dropped, the meaning would be disrupted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 66, verses 6–8:

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is men and stones, over which are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded.﴾ ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run before them and on their right. They will say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things competent."﴾

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families﴾. Its meaning is: make a means of protection between yourselves and the Fire. The explanation of the word has been given more than once before. His words, Exalted is He: "and your families" mean: by advising them, ordering them, and guiding them to obey Allah, Exalted is He. In a hadith: "Do not commit adultery, lest your family commit adultery." In another hadith: "May Allah have mercy on a man who said: O my family, your prayer, your fasting, your needy, your orphan." 

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿wuqūduhā﴾ with a fatha on the waw. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Talhah, 'Isa, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, and Abu Haywah read it with a damma. It is said that both have the same meaning. It is also said that the damma is a verbal noun (masdar) and the fatha is a noun (ism). It is related that the stones are brimstone stones, and this has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. It is also related that they are all kinds of stones. In some hadith: "'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, heard a moaning in a desert wasteland. He followed it until he reached a stone that was moaning and grieving. He said to it: What is wrong with you, O stone? It said: O Spirit of Allah, I heard Allah say: ﴿Its fuel is men and stones﴾, so I feared that I would be one of those stones. 'Isa, peace be upon him, marvelled at this and departed." It is likely that this meaning is in the Torah or the Gospel. That which he heard from the stone, when expressed in Arabic, would be this wording.

The description of the angels with harshness (ghilzah) means harshness in the hearts, a severe grip, and roughness, as Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you.﴾ And "shiddah" (severity) means strength. It is said that what is meant is their severity towards the disbelievers, so it has the meaning of harshness. Then He described them, Exalted is He, as being obedient to their Lord, and He repeated the meaning for emphasis with His words, Glorified is He: ﴿and do what they are commanded﴾. In His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and do what they are commanded﴾, there is an implication that they drive the disbelievers into the Fire with earnestness and free choice, and they are harsh with them. It is as if He said, after establishing this meaning: it will be said to the disbelievers, "Do not make excuses today," meaning that making excuses will not benefit you, and you are only recompensed for your deeds. So do not blame anyone except yourselves.

Then He commanded His servants to repent. Repentance (tawbah) is an obligation upon every Muslim. "Taba" means "returned." So the servant's repentance is his return from disobedience to obedience. Allah's repentance upon the servant is the manifestation of his righteousness and His blessing upon him in guiding him to obedience. The acceptance of the repentance of disbelievers, by consensus of the Ummah, is definitively established with Allah, Exalted is He. People have differed concerning the repentance of the sinner. The majority of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) hold that it is not definitively established that it will be accepted, nor is it obligatory upon Allah. The evidence for this is the supplication of each of the repentant ones for the acceptance of their repentance. If it were definitively established, there would be no point in supplicating for its acceptance. The apparent meanings of the Qur'an on this matter all carry the sense of will (mashi'ah). It is narrated from Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari that he said: when the conditions of repentance are fully met, Allah, Exalted is He, is definitively to accept it, because He has informed of that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an adherence to the apparent meanings of the Qur'an, and the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilah) have agreed upon this view. Repentance is regret over a past disobedience, and resolve to abandon its like in the future. This is for one who is able. As for one who is not able, such as a castrated man in regard to adultery, regret alone suffices him. Repentance is an act of worship like prayer and others. So when the servant repents, his repentance is achieved with its conditions and accepted, and then he returns to sin, his first repentance is not invalidated by the relapse. Rather, it is like all other acts of worship that have been performed.

"Nasūh" is an intensive form (bina' mubalaghah) from "nusḥ" (sincere advice), meaning: a repentance that gives sincere advice to its owner and guides him. The majority read "nasūḥan" with a fatha on the nun. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, Kharijah from Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and 'Isa read "nusūḥan" with a damma on the nun, and it is a verbal noun. It is said: "nasaḥa yansahu, nasāhatan wa nusūḥan," as al-Zajjaj said. So the repentance is described with a verbal noun, like "al-'adl" (justice) and "al-zūr" (falsehood) and the like. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The sincere repentance is that one repents and then does not return, and does not desire to return. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is that the earth becomes constricted upon you despite its vastness, like the repentance of those who were left behind.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps your Lord will...﴾, the verse, is an expression of hope (tarjiyah). It has been narrated that "perhaps" (asā) from Allah, Exalted is He, is binding. The governing element for "the Day" (yawma) is "will admit you."

It is narrated concerning the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾, that Muhammad (ﷺ) pleaded concerning the matter of his Ummah. Allah, Exalted is He, revealed to him: If you wish, I will make their reckoning yours. He said: O Lord, You are more merciful to them. Allah, Exalted is He, said: Then I will not disgrace you concerning them. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet﴾. Disgrace (khizy) is the hateful thing that leaves a person bewildered, ashamed, and distressed, by seeing his deficiency or the evil of his station.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and those who believed with him﴾ may be in conjunction with "the Prophet," so the believers would also be free from disgrace. It may also be a new beginning (ibtida'), with "their light runs before them" as its predicate sentence, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would remain singled out and preferred by being one who is not disgraced. The discussion of the parallel of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿their light runs before them and on their right﴾ has already been given. Sahl ibn Sa'd read "bi-'imānihim" with a kasra on the hamzah. As for their words, "Perfect for us our light," al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: this is when they see the extinguishing of the light of the hypocrites, as explained previously. It is also said: whoever is given light only to the extent of seeing the place of his feet says this.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 66, verses 9–10:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Allah sets forth an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, and [their husbands] could not avail them at all against Allah. And it was said: "Enter the Fire along with those who enter."﴾

This verse emphasizes the command of jihad (striving in the cause of Allah) and its obligation, which was mentioned earlier. The meaning is: persist in fighting the disbelievers with the sword, and strive against the hypocrites by enforcing the ḥudūd (the prescribed penalties) upon them and by striking them for all their crimes, whenever there is strong suspicion against them. Allah the Exalted did not specify for His Messenger ﷺ any hypocrite whose hypocrisy was certain, because the profession of faith that they displayed kept their affair ambiguous and made them resemble the sinners of the Ummah. The "harshness toward them" means severity of heart, rebuke, and little gentleness toward them. al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "wa-aghliẓ" (وَأغْلِظْ) with a kasra on the lām and a hamzat al-qaṭʿ (the open hamza), so that it is an imperative of the fourth form (ʾafʿal) instead of the sixth form (ghaliẓa).

These two examples, one for the disbelievers and one for the believers, mean that whoever disbelieves, nothing from Allah will avail him, and no burden will benefit him even if he is attached to the strongest of means; and that whoever believes, no one can prevent him from attaining the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted, even if he is in the worst of origins and the lowest of states. Some people said that in the two examples there is a lesson for the wives of the Prophet ﷺ when their reproach had preceded. This is far-fetched, because the text states that the examples are for the disbelievers, which rules this out.

People differed concerning the betrayal of these two women. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: they betrayed them in matters of disbelief. As for the wife of Noah, she used to tell the people that he was mad. As for the wife of Lot, she used to tell his people whenever a guest arrived, so that she would inform them of him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: "No wife of a prophet ever committed adultery, and the prophets, peace be upon them, were never tested through their wives with this." al-Ḥasan, in the book of al-Naqqāsh, said: they betrayed them by disbelief, by adultery, and by other things.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhūr) read "yughniyā" (يُغْنِيا) with a yāʾ. Bishr ibn ʿUbayd read "tughanniyā" (تَغَنِّيا) with a tāʾ on top (from above).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 66, verses 11–12:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people." And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was of the devoutly obedient.﴾

The wife of Pharaoh, whose name is "Asiya." Her words "and his deeds" (wa-'amalihi) mean: and his disbelief and what he was upon of misguidance. This is the view of all the commentators (mufassirun). Most commentators said: it means: from his injustice, his punishment, and his torment of me. It is related regarding this that Pharaoh learned of her belief in Musa (peace be upon him), and that she loved to be victorious. So he sent a group of people to her and said: "If you see from her that, then flatten her on the ground, stake down her hands and feet, and throw the largest rock upon her. And if you do not see that, then she is my wife." He said: The people went, and when she sensed the evil from them, she made these supplications, so Allah took her soul, and those people placed the rock upon a body with no spirit in it. Other than this has been related, which is lengthy, and I have abridged it because it is not authentic. Others said, in the book of al-Naqqash: "wa-'amalihi" is a metaphor for sexual intercourse and lying together, and this is weak.

People differed regarding the chastity (al-farj alladhi ahsanat) that Maryam, peace be upon her, guarded. The majority said: it is the opening (farj) of the garment she was wearing, and that she was a young girl, and that Jibril (peace be upon him) breathed the spirit into her through the collar of the garment. Others said: it is the private part of the body (al-farj al-jarihah), and the expression "ahsanat" (guarded) in the case of the private part is used in its literal sense, and in this case it is used in its proper meaning. Ihsan means guarding it. When we take it to mean the opening of the garment, the expression "ahsanat" is used figuratively, in that she guarded it and protected it, and in that it became a passage for her child.

His, the Exalted, words "fa-nafakhna" (so We breathed) refer to the action of Jibril (peace be upon him) in the literal sense. If someone holds that the breathing is the action of Allah, the Exalted, then it is a figurative expression for His creating and originating the child in her womb. This is likened to breathing, which by its nature moves a thing gently and softly. His, the Exalted, words "min ruhina" (of Our spirit) are an attribution of the created to the Creator and of the owned to the Owner, as you say "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah." Likewise, the spirit, in its whole category, is the spirit of Allah.

The majority read "wa-saddaqat" with a doubled dal. Abu Mijlaz read it with the dal lightened. The majority of people read "bi-kalimat" in the plural, and al-Jahdari read "bi-kalimah" in the singular. As for the singular, it strengthens the view that it refers to the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him), and it is possible that it refers to the category, which is the Torah. As for the one who reads in the plural, it strengthens that it refers to the Torah, and it is possible that it refers to the matter of 'Isa (peace be upon him). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Nafi' read "wa-kitabihi" in the singular. Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, and Kharija from Nafi' read "wa-kutubihi" with a damma on the ta' in the plural. Abu Raja' read it with the ta' sukun, "wa-kutbihi." All of this is intended to refer to the Torah and the Gospel.

"Al-qanitun" means the worshippers. The meaning is: she was among the people who were devoutly obedient in her worship and in the state of her religion.

The commentary on Surah [al-Tahrim] is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
